newsitem.title: USA: Senate approves Pena as energy secretary.
newsitem.headline: Senate approves Pena as energy secretary.

text.p: After delaying action for several weeks, the Senate Wednesday voted 99-1 to confirm Federico Pena as energy secretary.
Pena, transportation secretary in President Clinton's first term, was to be sworn in later Wednesday to be ready to testify at a congressional hearing Thursday, an Energy Department spokesman said.

While most senators said Pena was qualified, his nomination lagged in a dispute between several Republican senators and the White House over how to dispose of thousands of tons of radioactive waste from nuclear power reactors.
The Republican senators finally cleared Pena for a vote, saying they felt the White House was prepared to work with them on the radioactive waste issue.
"I want to applaud the Senate today for its strong support for Federico Pena to serve as our nation's new energy secretary," Clinton said in a statement.
"As transportation secretary, Federico Pena built consensus among communities, business and government and streamlined operations to reap benefits for all taxpayers," Clinton said.
Some Republicans had complained that Pena did not have the necessary background for overseeing the Energy Department's responsibilities of nuclear weapons programmes and energy programmes.
But most opposition stemmed from a dispute over the nuclear waste issue. In the final vote, only Minnesota Republican Rod Grams, who wants to abolish the Energy Department, voted against Pena.

"Secretary Pena faces many challenges, not the least of which is stopping the pile-up of high-level radioactive waste at 80 locations in 41 states," said Senate Energy Committee Chairman Frank Murkowski, an Alaska Republican.
"We need his leadership to help meet the federal government's obligation of solving the interim storage problem," Murkowski said.
Murkowski has pushed a bill to build a temporay storage site in Nevada to take the spent fuel, which the government legally becomes responsible for next year.
But the Clinton administration opposed the bill, saying it would divert resources from building a permanent storage facility, and that it would prejudge Nevada as the nation's nuclear waste dump.
Murkowski delayed the Energy Committee's vote on Pena while he tried to get some concessions from the White House to accept a nuclear waste interim storage bill.
He finally set the vote and supported Pena, saying Pena seemed willing to work with Congress on the issue.
